P1Q61.q: According to Aquinas, why must the angels have been made by God?
options: Because angels differ in essence from their existence, so they exist by participation and must be caused by God who alone exists essentially
Because angels are corporeal and all bodies require a maker
Because Scripture explicitly names each angel's creation
Because angels are eternal and eternal things require a first cause to sustain them
P1Q61.explanation: Aquinas argues that God alone is His own existence, while in everything else essence differs from existence; whatever exists by participation must be caused by what exists essentially, so the angels were made by God.

P1Q61.q: What does Aquinas say about the possibility that angels were created before the corporeal world?
options: It is heretical to think otherwise
It is more probable that angels were created at the same time as corporeal creatures, since angels are part of one universe with corporeal creatures
Angels must have existed for millions of years before matter
Scripture proves angels came a full day before matter
P1Q61.explanation: Aquinas holds the more probable opinion that angels and corporeal creatures were created together, since both unite to form one universe and no part is perfect when separated from the whole, though he does not condemn the contrary view.

P1Q61.q: Why does Aquinas say it was fitting for angels to be created in the highest corporeal place (the empyrean heaven)?
options: Because angels need physical rest
Because the empyrean heaven is eternal like God
Because spiritual creatures bear a relationship to and preside over corporeal creation, so they fittingly were created in the highest corporeal place
Because lower angels feared the light
P1Q61.explanation: Since spiritual creatures rule over corporeal nature, Aquinas reasons it was fitting for angels to be created in the highest corporeal place, presiding over all corporeal nature.

P1Q62.q: What does Aquinas identify as the angels' ultimate beatitude beyond natural contemplation?
options: Ruling over the corporeal world
Seeing God as He is, which exceeds the natural power of any created intellect
Endless philosophical contemplation of creatures
Perpetual praise without vision of the divine essence
P1Q62.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes a natural happiness attainable by contemplation from the higher beatitude of seeing God as He is, which is beyond the nature of every created intellect and requires grace.

P1Q62.q: Why did the angels need grace to turn toward beatitude, according to Aquinas?
options: Because the will's natural inclination only reaches what is proportionate to its nature, and beatitude with God is above nature
Because angels lack free will entirely
Because grace was needed only for the angels who sinned
Because beatitude is achieved purely through natural intellectual power
P1Q62.explanation: Aquinas explains that the will's natural inclination is directed to what suits its nature; since beatitude in God is above the angelic nature, a supernatural principle (grace) was needed to move the will toward it.

P1Q62.q: According to Aquinas, how quickly did an angel obtain beatitude after meriting it?
options: After a probationary period of testing
Only after many acts of increasing charity
Instantly after a single act of charity, because grace perfects nature according to its own mode, and angelic nature attains perfection at once rather than gradually
Never, since beatitude must be granted independent of merit
P1Q62.explanation: Because it is proper to angelic nature to receive perfection all at once rather than by stages, Aquinas holds that the angel was beatified immediately after the first meritorious act of charity.

P1Q63.q: Why can any created will, including an angel's, be capable of sin while God's will cannot?
options: Because only God's will has the divine will itself as its rule, whereas a created will's rectitude depends on being regulated by conformity to the divine will
Because angels have bodies that lead them into temptation
Because sin is simply a matter of external circumstance, not will
Because only humans, not angels, have true free will
P1Q63.explanation: Aquinas argues that sin is a deviation from due rectitude; only an act whose very rule is the agent's own will (as with God) cannot fail, whereas every created will must be regulated by the divine will and so is capable of falling short.

P1Q63.q: What does Aquinas identify as the first and only sin an angel could commit through inordinate affection?
options: Envy alone
Pride, since it is the sin of refusing due subjection to a superior in matters of spiritual good
Gluttony, adapted to spiritual pleasures
Sloth, from resisting the labor of contemplation
P1Q63.explanation: Since a spiritual nature can only be affected by things proper to spiritual goods, and sin here consists in not remaining subject to a superior when due, Aquinas concludes the first sin of the angel could only be pride.

P1Q63.q: In what sense, according to Aquinas, did the devil desire to be 'as God'?
options: He sought equality with God in nature, believing it possible

He sought likeness to God (e.g., by his own power attaining beatitude or ruling), not equality, since equality was known by him to be impossible and contrary to natural desire to preserve one's own nature
He wanted literally to replace God as creator of the universe
He desired only bodily pleasures superior to God's
P1Q63.explanation: Aquinas explains the devil could not have sought strict equality with God, which he knew by natural knowledge to be impossible; rather he desired a certain likeness to God, improperly, such as attaining beatitude by his own power.

P1Q64.q: According to Aquinas, is the will of the demons obstinate in evil?
options: No, demons can still repent at any time
Yes, contrary to Origen's view that every created will remains changeable, Catholic Faith holds the demons' will is fixed obstinately in evil just as the good angels are confirmed in good
Only some demons are obstinate, others are not
Obstinacy applies only to the highest demon, not the rest
P1Q64.explanation: Aquinas rejects Origen's opinion that every created will can always turn to good or evil, affirming instead that the will of demons is obstinate in evil, just as the good angels' will is confirmed in good, since everlasting stability belongs to true beatitude and its opposite.

P1Q64.q: Can sorrow exist in demons, according to Aquinas?
options: No, since demons lack any appetite whatsoever
Yes, understood as a simple act of will resisting what is or is not, since demons will things to be otherwise than they are and are deprived of the happiness they naturally desire
No, sorrow is purely a bodily passion and demons are incorporeal
Yes, but only as physical pain from fire
P1Q64.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes sorrow as a passion of the sensitive appetite (impossible in demons) from sorrow as a simple act of will resisting what is or is not; in this sense demons do experience sorrow, since they are deprived of desired happiness and resent many things that are.

P1Q64.q: Why does Aquinas say the demons have a twofold place of punishment, including our dark atmosphere?
options: Because demons enjoy tormenting themselves in various locations
Because hell punishes them for their sin, while the atmosphere serves Divine providence's use of demons to test and exercise mankind, so their service continues within the natural order
Because demons cannot fit in hell all together
Because Scripture never mentions hell at all
P1Q64.explanation: Aquinas reasons that besides hell (due to their sin), demons are permitted in the dark atmosphere so that, in tempting men, they still serve God's providence in indirectly procuring man's welfare through trial.

P1Q65.q: How does Aquinas refute the view that an evil principle, not the good God, created visible/corporeal things?
options: By citing only Church authority without argument
By showing that being is common to all things, however different, and there must be one principle of being from which all things—visible and invisible—receive their existence
By arguing that corporeal things are illusions and not really created
By claiming the objection was never actually raised by heretics
P1Q65.explanation: Aquinas argues that since diverse things share being in common, and things diverse in nature cannot unite of themselves, there must be one single cause of being for all things, visible and invisible—refuting the idea of a separate evil creator of corporeal things.

P1Q65.q: How does Aquinas respond to Origen's claim that corporeal creatures were made only to punish sinning spiritual creatures?
options: He agrees fully with Origen's position
He rejects it as erroneous, noting Scripture says God saw that each corporeal creature was good, implying they were made because it was good for them to exist, not merely as punishment
He says corporeal creation predates spiritual creation entirely
He argues Origen was correct only regarding animals, not plants
P1Q65.explanation: Aquinas rejects Origen's view as contrary to Scripture, which states after each corporeal creature's production that 'God saw that it was good,' implying corporeal creatures exist because their being is good, not merely as a penal measure.

P1Q65.q: What is Aquinas's verdict on the claim that corporeal creatures were produced by God only indirectly, through a chain mediated by angels?
options: He affirms it, since angels are perfect intermediaries
This position is untenable, since creation—the production of matter itself—can only be done by God alone, and the imperfect (matter) must exist before intermediate production could occur
He says it applies only to living corporeal creatures
He considers it a matter of indifferent theological opinion
P1Q65.explanation: Aquinas holds it is impossible for corporeal creatures to proceed through angelic mediation, since creation of matter itself is proper to God alone, and nothing can be created except immediately by God.

P1Q66.q: According to Aquinas's own resolution regarding formless matter, did primary matter ever exist entirely without any form, even briefly?
options: Yes, matter existed in total formlessness for eons before God imposed order

No, primary matter was not created altogether formless nor under one common form, but was created straightaway under distinct forms; only priority in nature/origin, not in time, can be attributed to its formlessness
Yes, but only during the first hour of creation
The question is irrelevant since Aquinas denies matter exists at all
P1Q66.explanation: Aquinas concludes that positing wholly formless matter existing in time before receiving form is self-contradictory (being in act without any act/form), so formlessness precedes formation only in the order of nature or origin, not in duration—though he notes other holy writers used 'formlessness' differently, to mean lack of due beauty, which did precede in time.

P1Q66.q: Regarding whether all corporeal things share the same primary matter, what does Aristotle's argument from natural movement establish?
options: That all matter is identical since all bodies eventually corrupt

That heavenly bodies, having a distinct natural movement (circular, without contrariety) unlike the elements' movements, have a different nature from the elements, against Plato's view of one common matter for all bodies
That circular movement proves heavenly bodies are alive
That Aristotle agreed entirely with Plato on this point
P1Q66.explanation: Aquinas notes Aristotle disproved Plato's view of a single common matter for all bodies by showing that the heavenly bodies' natural circular movement, free of contrariety, differs essentially from the elements' contrary movements, implying a different nature and matter for incorruptible heavenly bodies.

P1Q66.q: What best explains Aquinas's account of why the empyrean heaven is called 'fiery' (empyrean)?
options: Because it is scorching hot like ordinary fire
Because it was the site of the fall of the rebel angels
Because it signifies a fitting beginning of bodily glory, luminous and free from corruption from the outset, named for its brightness rather than for heat
Because ancient astronomers observed literal flames there
P1Q66.explanation: Aquinas explains that the empyrean heaven is called fiery on account of its brightness, not heat, fittingly marking from the beginning of the world an anticipation of the bodily glory expected after the Resurrection.

P1Q67.q: When Aquinas discusses whether the word 'light' can properly be applied to spiritual things, what does he conclude?
options: 'Light' can never be applied to spiritual realities in any sense
In its strict primary sense 'light' applies metaphorically to spiritual things, but in its extended sense (denoting manifestation of any kind) it can be properly applied to spiritual things
'Light' is a purely physical term with no extended meaning
Only Scripture, never philosophy, can use 'light' of spiritual things
P1Q67.explanation: Aquinas compares 'light' to 'sight,' noting that words originally tied to sense perception can be extended properly to broader meanings; taken as manifestation generally, 'light' can properly, not just metaphorically, apply to spiritual things.

P1Q67.q: Which of Aquinas's three reasons shows that light cannot be a body?
options: Light cannot be a body because two bodies cannot occupy the same place simultaneously, yet light and air do; also its diffusion is instantaneous rather than a local movement through intervening space, and light does not undergo generation/corruption as bodies do
Light must be a body because it can be reflected like a ball
Light cannot be a body because it has no color
Light is definitely a body because Augustine calls it 'the first among bodies' without qualification
P1Q67.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons: place (two bodies cannot coexist in one place, but light and air do), movement (light's diffusion is instantaneous, unlike a body's local movement through space), and generation/corruption (light does not require corrupting a body's matter when a light source is removed).

P1Q67.q: According to Aquinas's own conclusion, what kind of reality is light?
options: A separately subsisting spiritual substance
An active quality consequent upon the substantial form of the sun (or another self-luminous body), analogous to how heat is a quality consequent on the substantial form of fire
A pure accident with no cause whatsoever
The very substantial form of the air itself
P1Q67.explanation: After rejecting the views that light is either a mere intentional likeness or a substantial form, Aquinas concludes that light is an active quality flowing from the substantial form of a luminous body, just as heat flows from the substantial form of fire.

P1Q68.q: What guiding principle does Aquinas (following Augustine) lay down for interpreting disputed physical details in Genesis, such as the firmament?
options: Scripture's literal wording must always override any other consideration, with no room for reinterpretation

Hold the truth of Scripture without wavering, but since Scripture can bear multiple senses, hold a particular explanation only tentatively, ready to abandon it if shown false, so as not to expose Scripture to ridicule
Scientific findings should always be dismissed if they conflict with any patristic commentary
Only allegorical readings of Genesis are permissible
P1Q68.explanation: Aquinas cites Augustine's two rules: hold the truth of Scripture firmly, but hold particular physical explanations only provisionally, being willing to abandon a reading proven false, so unbelievers are not given occasion for ridicule.

P1Q68.q: Regarding the waters said to be 'above the firmament,' what is Aquinas's approach?
options: He denies outright that any such waters exist, contradicting Genesis

He affirms, following Augustine, that Scripture's authority assures us such waters exist in some sense, though their exact nature is disputed among commentators (spiritual, elemental, vaporous, or otherwise)
He insists they must be literal ocean water held up only by a miracle, with no natural explanation possible
He says 'waters above the firmament' refers exclusively to angels
P1Q68.explanation: Aquinas holds firmly, on Scripture's authority as Augustine states, that waters above the firmament exist in some mode, while surveying differing opinions (Origen's spiritual substances, elemental water, vapor, or matter in general) about their precise nature.

P1Q68.q: How does Aquinas reconcile Basil's and Chrysostom's differing statements about the number of heavens?
options: He says one of them must simply be wrong and rejects Chrysostom entirely

The difference is more nominal than real: Chrysostom uses 'heaven' for the whole body above earth and water as a single unit, while Basil, noting distinct parts within that body, speaks of several heavens
He says heaven is purely metaphorical and neither author means anything literal
He claims Basil later retracted his view to agree with Chrysostom
P1Q68.explanation: Aquinas reconciles the apparent disagreement by noting Chrysostom treats the whole supralunar body as one heaven while Basil, attending to its several distinct parts, speaks of many heavens—so the difference is verbal rather than substantive.

P1Q69.q: Following Augustine's interpretation as Aquinas presents it, what kind of order governs the sequence of the 'days' of creation?
options: A sequence of duration only, each day being exactly one literal day
An order of origin and nature rather than duration, so that the formation described on successive days need not follow one another in time
No order at all; the days are randomly arranged
An order based purely on the size of what was created
P1Q69.explanation: Aquinas explains that, per Augustine, the sequence of days in the works of distinction reflects an order of origin and nature—higher realities are recorded before lower—not necessarily a temporal sequence of literal successive days.

P1Q69.q: Regarding the production of plants on the third day, how does Augustine's view differ from that of other commentators, as Aquinas presents it?
options: Augustine holds plants sprang up fully grown in their actual species on the third day, while others deny plants existed until much later

Augustine holds the earth received on the third day only the causal power to produce plants (produced actually later, through propagation), while other commentators hold plants were actually produced in their species then
There is no difference; all commentators agreed completely
Augustine denied that plants were created by God at all
P1Q69.explanation: Aquinas notes that Augustine, appealing to Genesis 2:4-5, holds plants were created 'in their causes' on the third day (the earth receiving the power to produce them), while other commentators hold the actual species of plants appeared then, with only propagation left as ongoing governance.

P1Q69.q: What twofold formlessness of the earth does Aquinas say came to an end on the third day?
options: Formlessness due to darkness, and formlessness due to cold
The earth being invisible/void because covered by water, and shapeless/empty for lack of the adornment plants would give it
Formlessness of the firmament and formlessness of the stars
There was only one kind of formlessness, not two
P1Q69.explanation: Aquinas explains the earth's formless state was twofold: covered by waters (invisible/void) and lacking the beauty plants provide (shapeless/empty), both aspects ending on the third day through the gathering of waters and the production of plants.

P1Q70.q: How does Aquinas distinguish the 'work of adornment' (including the fourth day's lights) from the earlier 'work of distinction'?
options: They are identical works with different names

The work of distinction perfects things intrinsically (giving substantial form or due order), while adornment concerns what is extrinsic, akin to how a man's perfection lies in his own parts but his adornment lies in his clothing
Adornment happened before distinction chronologically
Adornment refers only to angelic beauty, not corporeal things
P1Q70.explanation: Aquinas compares the works: distinction perfects heaven and earth in what belongs to them intrinsically, while adornment concerns things extrinsic to them—illustrated by the analogy of a man's own parts versus his clothing—fittingly realized through the mobile things (lights, birds, fish, animals) of the later days.

P1Q70.q: What reason does Moses (per Aquinas) chiefly give for the lights' creation, among several possible reasons for corporeal creatures existing?
options: Their usefulness to man, in order to draw the people away from idolatrous worship of the sun, moon, and stars
Their role in generating heat exclusively
Their function purely as decoration with no practical use
Their necessity for the angels' own benefit
P1Q70.explanation: Aquinas notes that although corporeal creatures can be considered in relation to their own act, to other creatures, to the universe, or to God's glory, Moses specifically emphasizes the lights' usefulness to man, so as to turn the Israelites away from idolatrous worship of the heavenly bodies.

P1Q70.q: On the question of whether the heavenly lights are living beings, what is Aquinas's stated position?
options: He definitively affirms they are alive, agreeing fully with the Platonists
He definitively denies they have any life, agreeing fully with Basil and Damascene

He notes the diversity of opinion among philosophers and Doctors (Anaxagoras denying life, Platonists and Origen/Jerome affirming it, Basil/Damascene denying it) and reports that Augustine leaves the question in doubt
He claims Scripture settles the question explicitly and no doubt remains among any authorities
P1Q70.explanation: Aquinas surveys the conflicting opinions of philosophers and Church authorities on whether heavenly bodies are alive, noting that Augustine leaves the matter undecided, only suggesting that if they are alive their souls would be akin to angelic nature.

P1Q71.q: How does Aquinas describe the order of the fifth day's work relative to the days of distinction?
options: The fifth day has no correspondence to any earlier day
As the second day distinguished the intermediate body (water), the fifth day, in the middle of the adornment triad, adorns that same intermediate body through the production of birds and fishes
The fifth day corresponds to the sixth day, not the second
Fish and birds were created before the waters existed
P1Q71.explanation: Aquinas explains the work of adornment mirrors the work of distinction: just as the second day distinguished water as the intermediate body, the fifth (middle) day of adornment fittingly produces birds and fishes to adorn that same intermediate element.

P1Q71.q: How does Augustine's view on the production of fish and birds, as reported by Aquinas, differ from that of other commentators?
options: Augustine holds they were produced actually in their full species, others say only potentially
Augustine holds that the nature of the waters produced them only potentially on the fifth day, while other writers hold fish and birds were actually produced then
There is no reported disagreement on this point
Augustine denies fish and birds were ever produced by water
P1Q71.explanation: Just as with plants, Aquinas notes Augustine holds that fish and birds were produced by the waters only potentially on the fifth day, in contrast to other holy writers who held they were actually produced then.

P1Q71.q: Why does Aquinas see a parallel between the mention of light/lights on the fourth day and the mention of waters/firmament on the fifth day?
options: It is coincidental and has no theological significance
Moses draws the parallel deliberately, to show the fourth day corresponds to the first (light) and the fifth corresponds to the second (waters/firmament), matching adornment days to distinction days
Because the fourth and fifth days are actually the same day retold
Because water and light are made of the same substance
P1Q71.explanation: Aquinas observes that just as Moses mentions light and the lights together to link the fourth day to the first, he mentions the waters and firmament on the fifth day to link it to the second day of distinction.

P1Q72.q: Why does the sixth day, on which land animals are produced, correspond to the third day, according to Aquinas?
options: Because both days involve water primarily
As the third day distinguished the lowest body (earth) from water, the sixth day adorns that same lowest body, the earth, through the production of land animals
There is no correspondence; Aquinas sees the sixth day as unique
Because six is twice three numerically, with no other reason given
P1Q72.explanation: Aquinas explains that the sixth day, on which the earth (the lowest body) is adorned by land animals, corresponds to the third day, on which the earth was distinguished as dry land—hence 'the earth is mentioned in both places.'

P1Q72.q: Regarding the production of land animals, what position does Aquinas attribute to Augustine, paralleling his view on plants and marine life?
options: Augustine says land animals appeared actually in full species on the sixth day
Augustine says the production of land animals on the sixth day was potential, the earth having received the power to produce them, rather than an actual production of complete species that day
Augustine denies land animals were ever created
Augustine agrees fully with all other holy writers on this point
P1Q72.explanation: Aquinas notes that, consistent with his view on plants and on fish and birds, Augustine holds the earth's production of land animals on the sixth day was potential rather than actual, while other holy writers maintain it was actual.

P1Q72.q: What overall principle links the third and sixth days in Aquinas's schema of the six days' work?
options: Both days deal with celestial bodies
The lowest body (earth), distinguished on the third day, receives its adornment (animals) on the sixth day, completing the parallel structure between distinction and adornment
The third and sixth days are unrelated by design
Both days were originally the same day in the Hebrew calendar
P1Q72.explanation: Aquinas's overall schema pairs each day of distinction with a corresponding day of adornment: the third day distinguishes earth as dry land, and the sixth completes its adornment through the production of animals that move upon it.

P1Q73.q: What distinction does Aquinas draw between the 'first' and 'second' perfection ascribed to the seventh day?
options: There is no such distinction; perfection is a single simple concept

The first perfection is the substantial completeness of a thing (the form of the whole with all its parts), while the second perfection is the end attained by operation; the seventh day marks the first perfection of the universe, with final perfection (beatitude) reserved for the world's consummation
Both perfections refer to physical size
The seventh day represents only the second, final perfection of the saints
P1Q73.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the first perfection (a thing's substantial completeness, achieved by having its parts complete) from the second (the end attained through operation, i.e. the Saints' beatitude); the seventh day marks the first perfection—the completed universe at its founding.

P1Q73.q: In what sense does Aquinas say God 'rested' on the seventh day, given that rest is properly opposed to bodily movement?
options: God did not truly rest; the text is purely figurative and means nothing

'Rest' is understood in two senses applied to spiritual things: cessation from producing new kinds of creatures (God made no new species after day six), and the satisfaction of desire (God rested in the sense that His goodness, terminating in creatures, had no further object to attain)
God rested because He was physically tired from the work of creation
God's rest refers only to Christ's rest in the tomb
P1Q73.explanation: Aquinas explains that movement and rest, applied analogically to spiritual realities, yield two senses of rest: ceasing from producing new works, and the satisfaction of desire attained in one's goal; God is said to have rested in both senses on the seventh day.

P1Q73.q: How are the blessing and sanctifying of the seventh day connected to its being a day of rest, according to Aquinas?
options: They are unrelated, arbitrary additions to the text

They correspond to the two senses of rest already established: a thing is blessed insofar as it multiplies, and sanctified insofar as it is set apart or established firmly—fitting the completion and stability signified by God's rest
Blessing pertains only to plants and sanctifying only to animals
The blessing and sanctifying apply solely to the Sabbath observance among the Israelites
P1Q73.explanation: Aquinas ties the blessing and sanctifying of the seventh day back to the twofold sense of God's rest established in Article 2, associating blessing with fruitful multiplication and sanctification with being set apart in stable completeness.

P1Q74.q: How does Aquinas explain the reasoning behind dividing creation into six days, following the general schema he presents?
options: The number six was chosen arbitrarily by Moses with no theological significance

The days correspond to the perfection of the number six, the sum of its aliquot parts (1+2+3): one day for forming spiritual creatures, two for corporeal creatures, and three for the work of adornment
There were originally seven equal days with no differentiation of kind
Six days simply matches the number of visible planets known in antiquity
P1Q74.explanation: Aquinas notes that the perfection of the works corresponds to the perfection of the number six (equal to the sum of its aliquot parts 1, 2, 3): one day for spiritual creatures, two for corporeal, and three for adornment, according to Augustine's reckoning.

P1Q74.q: What is Augustine's distinctive position, as Aquinas reports it, on whether the six/seven days denote a real temporal succession?
options: Augustine agrees fully with those who hold seven distinct successive days

Augustine holds that all the days are really one day, understood as the angels' knowledge represented in a sevenfold aspect, denoting an order of things known rather than a temporal succession of production
Augustine denies that days have any meaning in Genesis at all
Augustine holds the days are exactly 24-hour periods, agreeing with the majority view
P1Q74.explanation: Aquinas reports that Augustine understands 'day' as angelic knowledge of God's works, so the seven days denote the natural order of things known to the angels rather than a real temporal succession of production, unlike the view of other expositors who held seven literal successive days.

P1Q74.q: According to Aquinas's reply regarding why 'God saw that it was good' is omitted for the second day's work, what is one reason offered?
options: Because the second day's work was evil
Because the work of distinguishing the waters was only begun on the second day and perfected on the third, so the approval given on the third day also covers the second
Because Scripture forgot to include it by scribal error
Because approval is given only for the first and last days, symbolically
P1Q74.explanation: Among several explanations Aquinas offers (following Rabbi Moses and others) for the omission of 'God saw that it was good' on the second day, one is that the work of distinguishing the waters begun on day two was only completed on day three, so the later approval retroactively covers day two as well.

P1Q75.q: What is Aquinas's central argument that the soul is not a body?
options: Because Scripture calls the soul invisible

Because the soul is the principle of life shown especially through knowledge and movement, and a corporeal principle cannot explain intellectual knowledge of all things, since a body has a determinate nature that would limit what it could know
Because bodies cannot move themselves
Because souls are found only in humans, not animals, and thus cannot be bodily
P1Q75.explanation: Aquinas rejects the ancient view that soul is corporeal, arguing (especially via the intellect's ability to know all bodies) that a bodily principle, having its own determinate nature, would be unable to know all things—so the soul, as principle of life and thought, is not a body.

P1Q75.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that the human soul is subsistent (able to exist per se)?
options: Because the soul feels pain in the body

Because the intellect can know all corporeal things, and this would be impossible if the intellectual principle had a determinate bodily nature of its own or operated through a bodily organ, so the intellectual principle must be incorporeal and subsistent
Because Aristotle explicitly used the word 'subsistent' for the soul
Because the soul is composed of the four elements in perfect balance
P1Q75.explanation: Since the intellect's grasp of all corporeal natures would be blocked if it had a determinate nature of its own (as a bodily organ would impose), Aquinas concludes the intellectual principle is incorporeal and subsistent, existing in its own right.

P1Q75.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that the souls of brute animals are not subsistent, unlike the human soul?
options: Because animals have no souls at all

Because every operation of the sensitive soul, unlike understanding, is always accompanied by change in a bodily organ, meaning sensation belongs to the composite of body and soul rather than to the soul alone, so brute souls have no per se operation and hence do not subsist
Because brute animals are inanimate objects
Because Plato proved that animals are purely mechanical
P1Q75.explanation: Following Aristotle against Plato, Aquinas holds that only understanding is performed without a bodily organ; sensation always involves bodily change, so it belongs to the composite, not the soul alone—hence animal souls lack a per se operation and are not subsistent like the human intellectual soul.

P1Q76.q: What is Aquinas's core argument that the intellectual soul is the substantial form of the human body?
options: Because Scripture calls man 'a living soul'

Because that whereby a thing primarily acts is its form, and since the soul is that whereby the body primarily lives, performs nourishment, sensation, movement, and understanding, the intellectual soul must be the form of the body
Because the soul is located in a specific bodily organ, the heart
Because Plato demonstrated this using the theory of Forms
P1Q76.explanation: Aquinas argues that a thing's form is that by which it primarily acts; since the soul is the primary principle by which the body lives, senses, moves, and understands, the intellectual soul (or intellect) must be the substantial form of the body, following Aristotle's demonstration.

P1Q76.q: Why does Aquinas hold that it is impossible for a single intellect to belong to all human beings (against a Platonic/Averroist-style unity)?
options: Because each person clearly has entirely separate physical brains

Because if intellect simply were man himself (per Plato) and were one, all individuals would collapse into being one man, distinguished only by accidental features like clothing, which is absurd; hence intellect must be multiplied per body
Because Aristotle never discussed the intellect's unity
Because the Church had already condemned this view by conciliar decree cited in the text
P1Q76.explanation: Aquinas shows the absurdity that would follow if one intellect belonged to all men by considering Plato's identification of man with intellect: individuals would then differ only by accidental features, like a man in a tunic differing from one in a cloak, which is untenable.

P1Q76.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that the soul must be present in every part of the body, not just one part?
options: Because the soul is spread out spatially like a fluid

Because the soul is not merely a motor (as the Platonists held) but the substantial form of the body, and since a substantial form gives actual existence to each part, not merely arranges them, the soul as form must actuate the whole body and each of its parts
Because Scripture describes the soul as filling the whole body like breath
Because otherwise the body would be too heavy for the soul to move
P1Q76.explanation: Since the soul is the substantial form of the body (not merely its mover), and a substantial form must give existence and act to each part of what it informs, Aquinas concludes the soul is wholly present in the whole body and in each part, unlike an accidental form of arrangement (like a house's form).

P1Q77.q: Why does Aquinas deny that the soul's essence is identical to its powers?
options: Because Scripture distinguishes soul from its faculties by name

Because if a power were identical with the soul's essence, it could not be that some operations belong to the soul alone (like understanding) while others belong to the composite (like sensation); powers are accidents of the soul, proper to it, distinct from its essence
Because powers change over time while the essence is eternal
Because Aristotle never used the word 'power' regarding the soul
P1Q77.explanation: Aquinas argues (with a fuller demonstration in the text) that the soul's power cannot be identical with its essence, since powers are principles of operation that must be distinguished according to differing acts and subjects, functioning as the soul's proximate operative principles rather than as its very essence.

P1Q77.q: Why must the human soul possess many and varied powers, according to Aquinas's comparison with lower and higher beings?
options: Because humans are physically the largest animals

Because things below man attain only limited, imperfect goodness with few powers, while man, capable of attaining universal and perfect goodness (beatitude) yet standing lowest among beings capable of it, requires many diverse powers and operations to reach that end
Because angels also need many powers, and man imitates angels perfectly
Because God arbitrarily multiplied human powers for variety's sake
P1Q77.explanation: Aquinas argues from a hierarchy of perfection: lower beings need few powers for their limited goodness, while man—capable of universal, perfect beatitude yet lowest among beings so capable—requires the widest variety of powers and operations, more than angels need.

P1Q77.q: On what basis does Aquinas say the powers of the soul are distinguished from one another?
options: By their location in different bodily organs alone

By their acts and objects, since a power is known through the act to which it is directed, and acts differ according to the different natures of their objects (as principle for passive powers, or as end/term for active powers)
By the order in which Scripture lists them
By their color and temperature as bodily qualities
P1Q77.explanation: Aquinas holds that since a power is defined in reference to its act, and an act's nature is diversified according to its object (as moving principle for passive powers or as end/term for active powers), the soul's powers are necessarily distinguished by their diverse acts and objects.

P1Q78.q: How does Aquinas rank the vegetative, sensitive, and rational operations of the soul in terms of transcending corporeal nature?
options: All three are equal in dignity and independence from the body

The rational operation is entirely independent of any bodily organ; the sensitive operation uses a bodily organ but not by virtue of a corporeal quality; the vegetative operation works through a bodily organ and by virtue of a corporeal quality (like heat), yet still exceeds mere corporeal nature by originating from an intrinsic principle
The vegetative soul is the highest since it governs growth
Sensitive operations require no bodily organ at all, only intellect does
P1Q78.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes three levels: rational operation transcends corporeal nature entirely (no organ involved), sensitive operation needs an organ but not a corporeal quality as such, and vegetative operation works through both an organ and a corporeal quality like heat, though still self-moving from within, unlike mere bodies.

P1Q78.q: What three powers does Aquinas assign to the vegetative part of the soul, and why?
options: Sight, hearing, and touch, since these preserve bodily life
Generative, augmentative, and nutritive—corresponding to acquiring existence, achieving due quantity, and preserving existence and quantity of the living body
Memory, imagination, and estimation
Intellect, will, and reason
P1Q78.explanation: Aquinas explains the vegetative part requires three powers directed to a threefold operation regarding the living body: the generative power (to acquire existence), the augmentative power (to reach due quantity), and the nutritive power (to preserve existence and quantity).

P1Q78.q: According to Aquinas, what determines the number and distinction of the exterior senses—organs, media, or something else?
options: The organs alone, since more organs simply produce more senses

Neither organs nor media alone properly explain it; rather, nature provides organs and media to suit the powers, since powers are not for the sake of organs, but organs exist for the sake of the powers
The location of each sense on the body's surface
Ancient astrological correspondences with the five known planets
P1Q78.explanation: Aquinas rejects explanations based purely on organs, media, or the physical composition of sensible qualities, insisting instead that nature furnishes diverse organs and media to serve the soul's powers, since powers exist prior to and are not caused by their organs.

P1Q79.q: Why does Aquinas hold that the intellect is a power of the soul rather than the soul's very essence?
options: Because only in God is His act of understanding identical with His very being; in all other intellectual creatures, since operation is not identical with their being, the intellect must be a power distinct from the soul's essence
Because Scripture never calls the soul 'intellect'
Because angels lack intellect but souls have it, proving a distinction
Because the intellect changes over a person's lifetime while essence does not
P1Q79.explanation: Aquinas reasons that a thing's essence is the immediate principle of its operation only when that operation is identical with its very being, which is true of God alone; in every other intellectual creature, including the human soul, the intellect is therefore a power, not the essence itself.

P1Q79.q: Why does Aquinas argue for the necessity of an active intellect, contrary to Plato's view?
options: Because Plato was simply mistaken about the existence of the soul

Because unlike Plato's separately subsisting intelligible Forms, Aristotle held that forms exist in matter and are only potentially, not actually, intelligible; thus something must be posited on the intellect's part to abstract and render them actually intelligible, requiring an active intellect
Because the active intellect is needed only to move the body, not to think
Because Scripture assigns intellect exclusively to angels, requiring a separate faculty in man
P1Q79.explanation: Since Aristotle (unlike Plato) held that forms exist embedded in matter and thus are only potentially intelligible, Aquinas argues an active power is needed to abstract species from material conditions and render them actually intelligible—this is the active intellect.

P1Q79.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that memory, as preserving intelligible species, is not a power distinct from the intellect?
options: Because memory belongs exclusively to the sensitive part of the soul, not the intellect at all

Because powers are distinguished by different formal objects, but the intellect regards its object under the common ratio of being without further differentiation, so retaining (memory) and receiving belong to the same passive power, not a separate one
Because Avicenna proved conclusively that no species can be preserved in any part of the soul
Because memory operates through a bodily organ, unlike the intellect
P1Q79.explanation: Since powers are differentiated by the formal aspect of their objects, and the passive intellect's object is being taken generally (undifferentiated), Aquinas concludes that retaining what is received (memory) belongs to the nature of the same passive power that receives it, not to a distinct faculty.

P1Q80.q: Why does Aquinas argue that an appetitive power must be assigned to the soul?
options: Because appetite is purely a bodily digestive function unrelated to the soul

Because every form is naturally followed by an inclination toward its own good; in beings with knowledge, this inclination rises to the level of an appetite responding to apprehended forms of other things, not just their own natural being, giving them a special likeness to God
Because Aristotle demanded a fourth soul-power for symmetry
Because plants and animals need appetite equally
P1Q80.explanation: Aquinas reasons that every form grounds a natural inclination (like fire's tendency to rise), and in knowing beings this is elevated: since they can receive the forms of other things through sense and intellect, they possess an appetite responding to what they apprehend, bringing a special likeness to God in Whom all things pre-exist.

P1Q80.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that the intellectual appetite (will) is a power distinct from the sensitive appetite?
options: Because the will operates without any object at all, unlike sensitive appetite

Because passive powers are differentiated according to their corresponding active/motive principles, and since what is apprehended by intellect differs generically from what is apprehended by sense, the appetite responding to each must likewise be distinct
Because the sensitive appetite is located in the soul while the will is located in the body
Because only humans have any appetite whatsoever, contrary to animals
P1Q80.explanation: Aquinas argues that since appetite is a passive power moved by its object, and passive powers are distinguished according to the generic difference of their corresponding active movers, the intellectual appetite (moved by what intellect apprehends) must be a distinct power from the sensitive appetite (moved by what sense apprehends).

P1Q80.q: In Aquinas's account, what makes a form's presence 'more perfect' in beings with knowledge compared to those without?
options: Knowing beings have larger, more complex bodies

In beings without knowledge, form only determines the thing to its own proper nature; in knowing beings, the form allows reception of the likenesses of other things as well (via sense and intellect), so such beings can, in a way, become all things and thereby approach a likeness to God
Knowing beings have no natural inclinations at all, unlike non-living things
There is no difference; Aquinas treats all forms as equally perfect
P1Q80.explanation: Aquinas contrasts unknowing beings, whose form fixes them only to their own nature, with knowing beings, whose form permits them additionally to receive the species of other things through sense and intellect—so the soul is, in a way, all things, approaching a likeness to God in Whom all things pre-exist.

P1Q81.q: According to Aquinas, why is sensuality identified with the sensitive appetite rather than sensitive apprehension?
options: Because apprehension and appetite are actually identical powers

Because the act of apprehension is likened to rest (the thing known comes to rest in the knower), while the act of appetite is likened to movement (the desirer is borne toward the thing desired); since 'sensual movement' names an appetite following apprehension, sensuality names the sensitive appetite
Because sensuality refers only to bodily temptation, unrelated to any power of the soul
Because Augustine defines sensuality as pure knowledge without desire
P1Q81.explanation: Aquinas reasons that apprehension's act completes in the thing apprehended being present in the knower (rest), while appetite's act completes in being borne toward the desired thing (movement); since 'sensual movement' denotes this latter movement, sensuality names the sensitive appetite.

P1Q81.q: Why does Aquinas divide the sensitive appetite into concupiscible and irascible powers?
options: Because Scripture lists exactly two categories of sin

Because besides an inclination to seek what is suitable and avoid what is harmful (concupiscible), there must also be an inclination to resist and overcome obstacles that hinder acquiring the suitable or that inflict harm (irascible), an arduous good or evil not reducible to the concupiscible alone
Because animals have two brain hemispheres
Because the irascible and concupiscible are simply two names for the same single power
P1Q81.explanation: Aquinas argues that beyond a basic inclination toward the suitable and away from the harmful (concupiscible), there must be a distinct power to resist and overcome obstacles to that pursuit (irascible), since its passions counteract and arise from the concupiscible's rather than reducing to it.

P1Q81.q: In what sense do the irascible and concupiscible appetites 'obey reason,' according to Aquinas?
options: They obey the universal reason directly, bypassing any mediating faculty

They are naturally moved by the particular reason (the cogitative power comparing individual intentions), which is itself guided by universal reason, so the sensitive appetite obeys reason rather than intellect strictly speaking, and can be modified by applying universal considerations
They do not obey reason at all in humans, only in angels
They obey the will directly and have no relation to reason
P1Q81.explanation: Aquinas explains that in man the sensitive appetite is moved by the particular reason (cogitative power), itself guided by universal reason drawing particular conclusions; hence the irascible and concupiscible are said to obey reason, and can be tempered by applying universal considerations, as anyone can experience in himself.

P1Q82.q: According to Aquinas, does the will desire everything of necessity?
options: Yes, the will always acts under absolute necessity like natural bodies

No: just as the intellect assents necessarily only to propositions necessarily connected to first principles, the will adheres necessarily only to what is necessarily connected to happiness (ultimately, the vision of God); particular goods not necessary for happiness are not willed of necessity
Yes, because coercion always determines the will's choices
No, because the will never desires anything necessarily, not even happiness itself
P1Q82.explanation: Aquinas draws a parallel: as intellect assents necessarily only to conclusions necessarily tied to first principles, the will adheres necessarily only to what is necessarily connected with happiness; particular, non-necessary goods do not move the will of necessity, though the beatific vision would.

P1Q82.q: How does Aquinas compare the intellect and the will in terms of dignity?
options: The will is always simply nobler than the intellect

The intellect is absolutely nobler, since its object (the abstracted idea of good) is simpler and more elevated in the mind, but the will can be relatively nobler when the thing willed is a reality greater than the soul itself (e.g., loving God is better than merely knowing corporeal things)
They are identical powers with no distinction in dignity
Neither power admits of comparison, since they operate on incommensurable objects
P1Q82.explanation: Aquinas argues that absolutely speaking the intellect is higher, since its object is more simple and abstract; but relatively, the will can surpass intellect when its object exists as a greater reality outside the soul—hence loving God is better than merely knowing corporeal things, though knowing corporeal things is better than merely loving them.

P1Q82.q: Why does Aquinas deny that irascible and concupiscible are distinct parts within the will (intellectual appetite)?
options: Because the will has no object at all

Because a power directed to its object under a common general notion is not multiplied according to particular differences contained under that notion, and the will's object (good in general, apprehended by intellect) is grasped as a simple, universal good without the sense-bound particularity that generates the irascible/concupiscible distinction in the sensitive appetite
Because Aristotle explicitly denied that the will has any object
Because irascible and concupiscible exist only in plants, not in intellectual creatures
P1Q82.explanation: Aquinas applies the principle that a power directed to an object under a common notion isn't subdivided by particular differences under that notion; since the will regards good universally as apprehended by intellect, it is not split into irascible and concupiscible as the sense-bound appetite is.

P1Q83.q: What is Aquinas's central argument for the existence of free-will in man?
options: Because Scripture commands obedience, proving freedom must exist

Because unlike things lacking knowledge (which act without judgment) or brute animals (which judge by natural, non-free instinct), man judges particular contingent matters through an act of reason's comparison, which can follow opposite courses, so man necessarily has free judgment
Because philosophers have always agreed unanimously that free-will exists
Because free-will is directly identical with the passions
P1Q83.explanation: Aquinas argues that man, unlike beings lacking knowledge or brutes following fixed natural instinct, judges particular contingent acts by reason, which in contingent matters can follow opposite courses (as in dialectical reasoning); since man is rational, he necessarily has free-will, otherwise counsel, commands, and rewards would be pointless.

P1Q83.q: According to Aquinas, is free-will (choice) primarily an act of the cognitive or appetitive power?
options: Purely cognitive, since choosing is simply a form of knowing

Principally an act of the appetitive power, since the proper object of choice is the means to an end, which falls under the nature of the good (the object of appetite), even though counsel from the cognitive power is also required for choice
Purely random and belongs to neither power
Equally divided with no power holding priority, per Aquinas's explicit final verdict
P1Q83.explanation: Though both counsel (cognitive) and acceptance of that counsel (appetitive) are involved in choice, Aquinas concludes that since choice's proper object (a useful means to an end) falls under the good as such, choice—and therefore free-will—is principally an act of the appetitive power.

P1Q83.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that free-will and the will are not two distinct powers, but one?
options: Because free-will and will refer to entirely unrelated faculties

Because just as intellect and reason belong to the same power (understanding first principles versus reasoning to conclusions), so willing the end and choosing the means belong to the same power; free-will is simply the will exercising the act of choice
Because Scripture uses the terms interchangeably without distinction
Because both terms simply mean 'grace' in Aquinas's technical vocabulary
P1Q83.explanation: Aquinas draws the parallel between intellect/reason (understanding principles vs. reasoning to conclusions, both belonging to one power) and will/free-will (willing the end vs. choosing means, likewise belonging to one power), concluding that will and free-will are the same power under different acts.

P1Q84.q: How does Aquinas explain the ancient philosophers' skepticism about certain knowledge of corporeal things?
options: They believed corporeal things were entirely fictional

Observing that all bodies are mobile and in continual flux (as Heraclitus held, using the image of never touching the same drop of a passing torrent twice), they concluded that certain knowledge of the true nature of things was impossible
They rejected the existence of the senses altogether
They held that only mathematical objects, not bodies, could be known
P1Q84.explanation: Aquinas explains that because early philosophers observed bodies as ever mobile and in flux, exemplified by Heraclitus's saying that one cannot touch the same passing drop of water twice, they concluded no certain knowledge could be had of such fleeting things.

P1Q84.q: According to Aquinas, does the soul understand bodies through its own essence (as some ancient philosophers held)?
options: Yes, this is Aquinas's own settled position

No; the ancient natural philosophers wrongly assumed knowledge required the knower to share the material nature of the known (e.g., soul made of fire, air, or the elements), failing to distinguish intellect from sense, whereas the truth is things are known immaterially, not materially, in the knower
Yes, because Plato's theory of ideas proves this conclusively
The question is meaningless since souls do not exist
P1Q84.explanation: Aquinas critiques the ancient view (that 'like is known by like' materially, leading thinkers like Empedocles to compose the soul of the four elements) as a failure to distinguish sense from intellect; genuine intellectual knowledge does not require the knower to materially share the nature of the thing known.

P1Q84.q: What does Aquinas conclude regarding innate ideas—does the intellect already possess species of things prior to experience?
options: Yes, the intellect is born with complete species of all things it will ever know

No; the intellect is originally in potentiality to the images (phantasms) that are principles of understanding, being reduced to act through sensation and then instruction or discovery, following Aristotle's view that the intellect has no innate species
Only mathematical species are innate; all others are acquired
Innate species exist only in angels, and the question does not apply to the human intellect at all, per Aquinas's flat denial that humans have intellects
P1Q84.explanation: Aquinas follows Aristotle in holding that the human cognitive soul begins in potentiality regarding both sensory and intelligible principles, moving from potency to act through the senses and then through instruction or discovery, rather than possessing complete innate ideas.

P1Q85.q: How does Aquinas explain the human intellect's characteristic way of knowing material things, given its 'middle' status between sense and angelic intellect?
options: The human intellect knows material things exactly as angels do, immaterially and without any process

The human intellect, unlike sense (bound to individual matter) and unlike angelic intellect (never tied to corporeal organs), knows a form existing in individual matter but not as existing in that individual matter—that is, by abstracting the form from the phantasms
The human intellect cannot know material things at all, only spiritual realities
The human intellect knows all things instantaneously and completely, like God
P1Q85.explanation: Aquinas places the human intellect between sense (which knows only individuals via a bodily organ) and angelic intellect (which knows immaterial forms directly); the human intellect properly knows a material form without the conditions of individual matter, i.e., by abstraction from phantasms.

P1Q85.q: Can the human intellect understand many different things simultaneously, according to Aquinas?
options: Yes, without any limitation whatsoever

It can understand many things at once only insofar as they are grasped under one intelligible species (as God understands all things in His one Essence), but it cannot simultaneously understand things known through different species, since one intellect cannot be perfected at once by diverse forms of one genus
No, the human intellect can only ever understand one thing at a time, without exception, even under a single species
Yes, but only two things at a time, never more, by a fixed natural law
P1Q85.explanation: Aquinas argues the intellect can grasp multiple things at once only if unified under a single intelligible species; but since distinct species belong to one genus (perfections of one faculty) and cannot simultaneously inform the same subject, understanding through different species cannot occur simultaneously.

P1Q85.q: Why does the human intellect necessarily understand by composition and division (i.e., forming propositions), according to Aquinas?
options: Because language requires grammatical subjects and predicates

Because, moving from potentiality to act like things generated, the human intellect does not grasp perfect knowledge in one single act but first apprehends the quiddity of a thing and then its properties, accidents, and relations, necessarily comparing them through composition and division
Because Aristotle commanded that all human thought be expressed in syllogisms
Because composition and division apply only to angelic intellects, not human ones
P1Q85.explanation: Aquinas explains that the human intellect, moving gradually from potency to act like generated things, first grasps a thing's quiddity and only later its properties and relations, necessarily comparing them by composing and dividing—the basis of discursive reasoning.

P1Q86.q: Can the human intellect know singular material things directly, according to Aquinas?
options: Yes, singulars are the intellect's primary and direct object

No, not directly and primarily, since the principle of singularity is individual matter, from which the intellect abstracts its species; the intellect knows the universal directly and knows the singular only indirectly, by a kind of reflection back on the phantasm
Yes, but only singulars that are morally significant
No, the intellect can never know singulars in any way, even indirectly
P1Q86.explanation: Since the intellect understands by abstracting species from individual (i.e., singularizing) matter, it grasps the universal directly; it knows the singular only indirectly, by reflecting back upon the phantasm from which the universal species was abstracted, as when forming 'Socrates is a man.'

P1Q86.q: Can our intellect actually (rather than merely potentially or successively) understand the infinite as a completed whole, according to Aquinas?
options: Yes, since intellect and its object are proportionate and the infinite is fully graspable as one whole

No; the infinite cannot be represented by one intelligible species (which would make it a finished whole, contradicting its nature) and can only be considered successively, one part after another, which can never be completed, so it cannot be known actually as a totality
Yes, but only by angels, never by the human intellect, and Aquinas makes no comment on human capacity here
No, the intellect can know absolutely nothing about the infinite, even potentially or successively
P1Q86.explanation: Aquinas argues the infinite is only potentially in the mind through successive consideration, never actually as a whole, since actual understanding requires one unifying species, but the infinite by definition always leaves something further to be taken and thus can never be completed.

P1Q86.q: How does Aquinas explain the intellect's relation to contingent things?
options: The intellect cannot know contingent things in any way whatsoever

Contingent things as such (tied to particular matter) are known directly by sense and only indirectly by intellect, while the universal and necessary principles underlying contingent things are known properly by intellect, so science of universal principles is always of necessary things even when the things themselves are contingent
Contingent things are known with total certainty and necessity by the intellect in every case
Only God, never the human intellect, can know anything about contingent things
P1Q86.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes contingency, arising from matter and known directly by sense, from the necessary universal principles underlying contingent things, known by intellect; thus science of universal principles is of necessary things, even though the contingent particulars themselves are known otherwise.

P1Q87.q: How does the human intellect come to know itself, according to Aquinas, in contrast to how immaterial substances know themselves?
options: The human intellect knows its own essence directly and immediately, exactly as immaterial substances do

Unlike immaterial substances that are intelligible by their own essence (since they are wholly in act), the human intellect—not itself the first object of its own act—knows itself only through knowing its own acts, which arise from knowing external material objects; thus self-knowledge is secondary and mediated by its acts
The human intellect never knows itself under any circumstances
The human intellect knows itself only through direct divine revelation, never through its own operations
P1Q87.explanation: Aquinas explains that whereas immaterial substances (fully in act by their essence) are intelligible through their essence, the human intellect's first object is the quiddity of a material thing; hence the intellect comes to know itself only secondarily, through reflecting on its own act of understanding that object.

P1Q87.q: According to Aquinas, how does the intellect come to know the act of the will?
options: The intellect cannot know the will's act, since will and intellect are entirely separate and incommunicable faculties

Since the will's act (an intelligible inclination) resides intelligibly in the intelligent subject as in its proper subject, whatever is intelligibly present in an intelligent subject is understood by that subject; hence the intellect knows the act of the will, both that one wills and the nature of that act
The will's act is known only through bodily sensation, never through intellect
Only angels can know the acts of a human will; humans cannot know their own will's acts
P1Q87.explanation: Aquinas reasons that the will's act, as an intelligible inclination following the understood form, exists intelligibly within the intelligent subject; since whatever is intelligibly present is understood by that subject, the intellect knows the will's act, both as to its occurrence and its nature.

P1Q87.q: What order of knowing does Aquinas identify for the human intellect regarding objects, acts, and powers?
options: Powers are known first, then acts, then objects

Objects are known before acts, and acts before powers, since for the human intellect the first known thing is the nature of a material object, the act of knowing that object is known secondarily, and the power itself is known through its act
All three (objects, acts, powers) are known simultaneously and equally in every case
Acts are known first, prior to any object, since acts are self-evident
P1Q87.explanation: Aquinas states that the human intellect knows objects first (the quiddity of material things), then knows its own act by which the object is known, and through that act comes to know the power (the intellect) itself, following the Philosopher's order: objects, then acts, then powers.

P1Q88.q: How does Aquinas evaluate Plato's claim that immaterial substances (Ideas) are the first and proper objects understood by the human intellect?
options: Aquinas fully endorses Plato's view without modification

Aquinas rejects it: for Plato, material things are known only because phantasy and sense mix with the mind, and the purer the intellect the more clearly it grasps immaterial truth directly—but Aquinas holds instead that in the present life our intellect's proper and first object is the quiddity of material things
Aquinas says immaterial substances are never known by humans in any way, in this life or after death
Aquinas says only angels can judge whether Plato was correct, leaving the question open
P1Q88.explanation: Aquinas summarizes Plato's view that immaterial Ideas are what we understand first and properly, with material knowledge being a corruption via sense and phantasy, but Aquinas's own position (developed through the question) is that in this life the intellect's proper object is the material thing's quiddity, and immaterial substances are known only imperfectly through material things.

P1Q88.q: Is God the first object known by the human mind, according to Aquinas?
options: Yes, since God is the cause of all things, He is necessarily what the mind grasps first

No; since in the present life the human intellect cannot even understand created immaterial substances, much less can it grasp the uncreated divine essence—God is known through creatures, and the first object of human knowledge is the quiddity of a material thing
Yes, because Augustine's illumination theory means we see all things directly in God, including God Himself as first known
The question is meaningless since Aquinas denies humans can know God in any way
P1Q88.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the human intellect in this life cannot grasp even immaterial created substances, it certainly cannot grasp the uncreated divine essence first; rather, per Romans 1:20, we know God through creatures, with material quiddity being the intellect's actual first object.

P1Q88.q: According to the Avempace-inspired view Aquinas reports, how might the intellect ascend from material things to knowledge of immaterial substances?
options: Through direct mystical vision unrelated to abstraction

By repeatedly abstracting whatever material residue remains in an already-abstracted quiddity; since this process of further abstraction cannot continue infinitely, it must terminate in an absolutely immaterial quiddity, yielding understanding of immaterial substance
By memorizing propositions about angels from Scripture
By observing the motion of celestial bodies directly with the senses
P1Q88.explanation: Aquinas reports Avempace's (via Averroes) view that since abstraction of quiddity from matter can itself be reapplied to whatever material element remains in the abstracted quiddity, and this process cannot proceed to infinity, it must eventually reach a wholly immaterial quiddity—constituting knowledge of immaterial substance.

P1Q89.q: What difficulty does Aquinas identify regarding whether the separated soul (after death) can understand anything?
options: There is no difficulty; the soul obviously understands nothing once separated from the body

If understanding by turning to phantasms belongs to the soul's very nature (not merely an accidental effect of embodiment, as the Platonists held), then since death does not change the soul's nature, it would seem the separated soul—now lacking phantasms to turn to—could understand nothing at all
The difficulty is whether the separated soul understands too much, overwhelming its capacity
The problem concerns only whether angels can communicate with separated souls, not whether souls can think
P1Q89.explanation: Aquinas frames the puzzle: unlike the Platonic view where phantasm-dependence is merely accidental to an embodied soul, if this dependence belongs to the soul's very nature, then after death—when phantasms are unavailable—the unchanged nature of the soul would seem to leave it unable to understand anything naturally.

P1Q89.q: According to Aquinas, does the separated soul know all natural things fully and clearly, similar to how angels know them?
options: Yes, separated souls know everything with the same clarity as the highest angels

No; being naturally inferior to angels, separated souls, even though they understand via divinely infused species (as angels do), receive from such species only a general and confused knowledge of natural things, not the perfect, proper knowledge angels have
No, separated souls know absolutely nothing about natural things under any mode
Yes, but only regarding mathematical truths, not physical natures
P1Q89.explanation: Aquinas argues that although separated souls, like angels, understand through species from divine illumination, their natural inferiority to angels means they receive only general, confused knowledge of natural things, whereas angels through the same kind of species attain perfect and proper knowledge.

P1Q89.q: Why, according to Aquinas, do separated souls of the dead not naturally know what happens on earth among the living?
options: Because God has permanently blinded all separated souls as a punishment

Because separated souls know singulars only insofar as they are determined to them by some vestige of prior knowledge, affection, or divine ordering, and souls of the dead are, by both divine order and their changed mode of existence, separated from the affairs of the living
Because the living deliberately hide their affairs from the dead through prayer
Because time does not exist for separated souls, making 'what happens on earth' a meaningless concept for them
P1Q89.explanation: Aquinas explains that separated souls know particular things only as they are determined toward them (by prior knowledge, affection, or divine disposition); since the dead are separated from the living by divine order and their new mode of existence among incorporeal substances, they do not naturally know earthly affairs, citing Gregory's and Augustine's agreement.

P1Q90.q: Why does Aquinas reject the idea that the human soul is made of the very substance of God?
options: Because Scripture explicitly forbids the phrase without giving a reason

Because the human soul is sometimes in potentiality to understanding, acquires knowledge from things, and has various powers—all incompatible with the Divine Nature, which is pure act, receives nothing from another, and admits no variety within itself
Because souls, unlike God, occupy physical space
Because only angels, not human souls, could plausibly be of the divine substance
P1Q90.explanation: Aquinas argues that the soul's characteristic potentiality (to acquire knowledge), its dependence on external things for that knowledge, and its multiplicity of powers are all incompatible with the Divine Nature, which is pure act without potentiality, reception from another, or internal variety.

P1Q90.q: Why must the rational soul be produced by creation rather than from any pre-existing matter?
options: Because the soul is not truly a substance and thus needs no special origin

Because the rational soul, unlike non-subsistent forms (accidents), is itself a subsistent form properly said 'to be' and 'to be made'; since it cannot be made from pre-existing corporeal matter (which would make it corporeal) or from pre-existing spiritual substance (which would mean transmuting one spiritual being into another), it can only come to be through creation
Because the soul is generated the same way plant and animal souls are, through natural biological processes
Because the soul is eternal and was never made at all
P1Q90.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes subsistent forms (like the rational soul, which properly 'is' and can be 'made') from non-subsistent forms/accidents; since the soul cannot arise from transmuting corporeal or spiritual pre-existing matter, its only possible mode of production is creation.

P1Q90.q: Why does Aquinas insist the rational soul must be created immediately by God alone, not through the mediation of angels?
options: Because angels are too holy to be involved in something as lowly as soul-making

Because only the first agent (God) can act without presupposing anything pre-existing, which is required for creation; every secondary cause, including angels, presupposes something derived from a prior cause and acts by producing change, not by creating, so the soul, produced without change in matter, must come immediately from God
Because it is impossible for immaterial beings like angels to act upon anything at all
Because Scripture names specific angels responsible for delivering souls, which Aquinas rejects as unbiblical embellishment
P1Q90.explanation: Aquinas reasons that only the first cause (God) can act without presupposing something already existing, i.e., can create; every secondary agent (including an angel) presupposes something from a prior cause and thus acts by change rather than creation—so since the soul is produced without any change in matter, it must come immediately from God alone.

P1Q91.q: Why does Aquinas say the first man's body is said to be made 'from the slime of the earth,' calling man a 'little world'?
options: Because man's body is literally composed of mud with no other elements

Because man, having a rational soul like spiritual substances and an equable temperament like the heavenly bodies, also contains the elements in his substance, with the higher elements (fire, air) predominating in power but the lower elements (earth, water, forming 'slime') predominating in quantity for balance
Because ancient near eastern mythology required this specific phrase
Because Adam's body was formed instantly without any material composition
P1Q91.explanation: Aquinas explains man contains a rational soul (like spiritual substances), an equable temperament (like heavenly bodies), and the elements themselves, with higher elements dominant in power and lower elements (earth and water, i.e., slime) dominant in quantity for balance—hence man is called 'a little world.'

P1Q91.q: Why does Aquinas insist the first human body could only have been formed immediately by God, not through any created instrumental power?
options: Because bodies cannot be formed by any power whatsoever, including God's

Because a form existing in matter can only be produced by another form existing in matter (composite by composite), and since no pre-existing body of the same species existed to generate the first human body, and only God can produce matter itself by creation, the first body had to come immediately from God
Because angels are physically incapable of touching matter
Because Scripture never mentions any process, only a single verbless command
P1Q91.explanation: Aquinas argues that forms in matter are only produced by other forms in matter (composite generating composite); since no prior human body existed to generate the first one, and only God can produce matter through creation, the first human body had to be made immediately by God, without instrumental causes.

P1Q91.q: How does Aquinas explain God's giving the human body its 'apt disposition,' using the analogy of an artist?
options: God gave the body absolutely the most beautiful possible material without regard to function

Like an artist who chooses iron rather than more beautiful glass for a saw because iron suits the saw's purpose, God gave each natural being the best disposition relative to its proper end, not the best disposition in an absolute sense, even if this involves some resulting limitation
God's artistry has no analogy to human artistry and operates on entirely different principles
The body's disposition is a matter of pure chance with no fitting design
P1Q91.explanation: Aquinas uses the example of a craftsman choosing iron over more beautiful glass for a saw because it serves the tool's purpose, arguing similarly that God gives each being the disposition best suited to its proper end, not the disposition that is best absolutely.

P1Q92.q: Why does Aquinas say woman was necessary as a 'helper' to man specifically in the work of generation, rather than as a general helpmate?
options: Because women are incapable of any other kind of assistance
