Because in perfect animals the active power of generation belongs to the male and the passive power to the female, and since man is ordered to an even nobler operation (intellectual activity) beyond mere generation, it was fitting for the female to be produced as a distinct helper specifically for generation, since another man could assist more efficiently in other kinds of work
Because Scripture gives no reason and Aquinas simply repeats the text without argument
Because woman was created solely to keep man from loneliness, unrelated to generation
P1Q92.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since man could be helped more efficiently by another man in other tasks, and since among perfect animals generation requires distinct active (male) and passive (female) powers, woman's specific role as helper pertains to generation, fitting man's further ordering toward intellectual life.

P1Q92.q: Why, according to Aquinas, could the human body of the first woman only be produced immediately by God, from the rib, rather than by natural generation?
options: Because natural generation of any human individual requires the determinate matter of human semen, and since ribs are not this determinate matter, only God, the Author of nature who can act outside nature's ordinary course, could produce a woman from a man's rib
Because women are naturally generated from any material whatsoever
Because Aquinas denies any special mode of the woman's origin at all
Because the rib itself was already a complete human body needing only reanimation
P1Q92.explanation: Aquinas argues that natural generation always proceeds from the determinate matter of human semen; since a rib is not this matter, producing a woman from a rib required God acting outside the ordinary course of nature, just as forming the first man from earth's slime did.

P1Q93.q: According to Aquinas (citing Augustine), what is the key distinction between 'likeness' and 'image,' relevant to whether man is God's image?
options: Likeness and image are entirely synonymous terms with no distinction

Wherever there is an image there is likeness, but likeness alone does not necessarily constitute an image; an image adds that it is copied from, or an imitation of, something else (as an egg resembling another egg is not thereby an 'image' of it, since it wasn't copied from it)
Image refers only to physical resemblance, likeness only to moral resemblance
Likeness applies only to angels, image only to humans, with no overlap
P1Q93.explanation: Aquinas cites Augustine that likeness is essential to but not sufficient for image; an image requires the further note of being copied from, or an imitation of, its exemplar, unlike mere similarity such as between two eggs of like appearance.

P1Q93.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that the image of God is found in man specifically according to the mind, not the body or other parts?
options: Because the mind alone is the seat of a 'trace' of God, not a true image

Because the intellect or mind is what makes the rational creature excel other creatures, and while a 'trace' likeness to God (like an effect representing a cause without specific likeness) is found throughout creation, the true 'image' (requiring likeness in species) is found in the rational creature specifically in the mind
Because the body is entirely excluded from any resemblance to God, even a trace
Because Aquinas denies image applies to any part of man, mind included
P1Q93.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes an 'image' (requiring specific likeness) from a mere 'trace' (an effect that represents its cause without attaining specific likeness, like ashes tracing fire); since intellect is what elevates rational creatures, the true image of God in man is found specifically in the mind.

P1Q93.q: Where does Aquinas locate the clearest image of the Trinity within the human soul?
options: In the soul's nutritive and sensitive powers alone

Primarily in the acts of the soul—since the Word cannot exist without actual thought, the image of the Trinity is found chiefly where the soul forms an internal word from knowledge and proceeds to love, and secondarily in the habits and powers that are principles of such acts
Exclusively in bodily gestures and external behavior
Nowhere in the soul; the Trinity's image exists only in the physical universe as a trace
P1Q93.explanation: Aquinas locates the image of the Trinity chiefly in the soul's acts—forming an inner word through actual thought (paralleling the Word's procession) and breaking forth into love (paralleling the Spirit's procession)—and secondarily in the habits and powers that virtually contain these acts.

P1Q94.q: Did the first man, in the ordinary state of his earthly life, see God through His Essence, according to Aquinas?
options: Yes, Adam had the beatific vision permanently before the Fall

No; since anyone seeing God's Essence would be so firmly established in love of God as to be unable to sin, and Adam did in fact sin, it follows he did not see God through His Essence in the ordinary state of that life
Yes, and this vision is precisely why Adam could still sin freely afterward
The question is meaningless since Adam is a purely symbolic figure for Aquinas
P1Q94.explanation: Aquinas reasons that seeing the Divine Essence (which is beatitude itself) would make it impossible to willingly turn away from God (i.e., to sin); since Adam did sin, he could not have seen God through His Essence in his ordinary earthly state.

P1Q94.q: Why does Aquinas hold that the first man, as originally created, possessed comprehensive knowledge fitting his role?
options: Because Adam had already experienced centuries of accumulated learning

Because in the natural order perfection precedes imperfection (as act precedes potency), and since man can be a principle for other men not only through bodily generation but also through instruction and governance, the first man's soul, like his body, was established in a perfect state fitting for teaching and governing others
Because Adam's knowledge was entirely revealed supernaturally with no natural basis whatsoever
Because Aquinas denies Adam had any special knowledge at all, being ordinary in every respect
P1Q94.explanation: Aquinas argues that since things are produced in their perfect state to serve as principles for others, and man can be a principle for other men through instruction and governance as well as generation, the first man's soul was established in a state of knowledge fit to instruct and govern others.

P1Q94.q: Could the first man, before sin, be deceived, according to the opinion Aquinas presents?
options: No, Adam had absolutely infallible knowledge of literally everything in existence, without exception

Regarding matters to which his knowledge extended, Adam could not be deceived in either a slight surmise or firm belief; but regarding matters beyond his knowledge, he could be deceived in the loose sense of holding a mistaken surmise without the assent of firm belief
Yes, Adam was constantly and totally deceived about everything, even before the Fall
Deception is impossible to define for pre-Fall humanity, so Aquinas declines to answer
P1Q94.explanation: Aquinas presents the view that within the scope of Adam's actual knowledge he could not be deceived at all, but regarding matters outside that scope he could hold a mistaken surmise (without firm assent), which is not blameworthy as long as he did not assent rashly.

P1Q95.q: According to Aquinas, was the first man created already possessing sanctifying grace?
options: No, grace is entirely unnecessary for any rational creature, including Adam
Aquinas holds, in keeping with the authority of many saints, that man possessed grace already in the state of innocence, rather than receiving it only later before he sinned
Grace was given to Adam only after he had already sinned, as a remedy
Adam possessed grace only briefly and lost it before creation was even complete
P1Q95.explanation: Aquinas reports and affirms, based on the authority of many saints, that the first man possessed grace already in his original state of innocence, rather than acquiring it at some later point before the Fall.

P1Q95.q: Which passions did Adam experience in the state of innocence, according to Aquinas?
options: All passions equally, including fear and sorrow, exactly as we experience them now
None whatsoever; Adam was entirely without any passions of the soul

Only passions regarding present or rightly-ordered future good (such as joy, love, desire, and hope), since no evil was present or threatened and no desired good was lacking; and unlike in us, these passions in Adam always followed reason's judgment rather than forestalling or resisting it, since his sensual appetite was wholly subject to reason
Only negative passions like sorrow and fear, since he anticipated the coming Fall
P1Q95.explanation: Aquinas explains that since no evil threatened Adam and no desired good was absent, he lacked passions like fear and sorrow, but he did have passions regarding present or rightly-ordered future good (joy, love, desire, hope)—and crucially, these always followed reason's judgment, since his lower appetite was wholly subject to reason, unlike our own disordered passions.

P1Q95.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that Adam, in the state of innocence, possessed all the virtues in some sense?
options: Because he directly witnessed the beatific vision, which grants all virtues automatically

Because the rectitude of the primitive state consisted in reason being subject to God and the lower powers subject to reason, and since the virtues are precisely those perfections directing reason to God and ordering the lower powers according to reason, this same rectitude required Adam to possess every virtue in some sense
Because virtues are entirely unnecessary before the Fall, and Aquinas denies Adam had any virtue at all
Because Adam inherited virtues genetically from no prior human ancestors, by a special miracle unrelated to grace
P1Q95.explanation: Aquinas reasons from the definition of virtue as ordering reason to God and regulating lower powers by reason; since the primitive state's rectitude consisted precisely in this order (reason subject to God, lower powers subject to reason), it follows that Adam possessed all the virtues in some sense.

P1Q96.q: Why does Aquinas hold that Adam had mastership over the animals in the state of innocence?
options: Because Adam was physically stronger than all animals

Because man's disobedience to God resulted, as punishment, in creatures naturally subject to him becoming disobedient; since this disobedience is a post-Fall punishment, it follows that before the Fall, since all animals are naturally subject to man, nothing naturally subject to him would have disobeyed him
Because animals worship humans as gods in Aquinas's account
Because Adam had no real mastership over animals even before the Fall, contrary to popular belief
P1Q96.explanation: Aquinas reasons backward from the punishment: since man's disobedience to God was punished by the disobedience of creatures naturally subject to him, it follows that before the Fall, nothing naturally subject to man (including animals) would have disobeyed him.

P1Q96.q: How does Aquinas explain the different modes of man's mastership over sensitive powers, natural powers, and lower creatures?
options: Man exercises identical mastership—by command—over everything without distinction

Man has mastership by 'commanding' over his own sensitive powers (irascible/concupiscible, which partly obey reason) and correspondingly over animals; but over his own natural powers and body, and correspondingly over plants and inanimate things, he has mastership only by 'using' them, not commanding them
Man has no mastership over his own body or natural powers at all, only over external creatures
Man's mastership over animals in paradise was purely symbolic, with no actual authority implied
P1Q96.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes mastership by commanding (which applies to the sensitive powers that partly obey reason, and correspondingly to animals) from mastership merely by using (which applies to man's own natural powers and body, and correspondingly to plants and inanimate things).

P1Q96.q: Would there have been inequality among men in the state of innocence, according to Aquinas?
options: No, absolutely no inequality of any kind would have existed among humans in paradise
Yes, at least inequality of sex (necessary for generation) and of age (since some would be born of others, and sexual union would not have been sterile) would have existed even in the primitive state
No, all humans would have been created simultaneously as identical adults with no differences whatsoever
Yes, but only inequality of intelligence, with all other differences excluded
P1Q96.explanation: Aquinas argues that some inequality was unavoidable even in the primitive state, since generation requires diversity of sex, and since children would be born of parents, differences of age would necessarily also exist, given that sexual union in paradise would not have been sterile.

P1Q97.q: In what sense would man in the state of innocence have been immortal, according to Aquinas?
options: Man's body was made of an inherently incorruptible substance, like the heavenly bodies

Not by an inherent incapacity for corruption in the body's nature, nor by an intrinsic power of the soul making the body incorruptible on its own, but by a supernatural force given by God to the soul, enabling it to preserve the body from corruption as long as the soul remained subject to God
Man was immortal only in the sense that his soul, not his body, would never perish, exactly as after the Fall
Immortality in paradise refers only to fame and memory, not actual bodily persistence
P1Q97.explanation: Aquinas explains three ways a thing can be incorruptible and situates man's paradisal immortality in the third: not by nature's inherent incorruptibility, but by a supernatural gift whereby the soul, remaining subject to God, was empowered to preserve the body from the corruption to which its material composition would otherwise be liable.

P1Q97.q: Why did the first man, though possessing an 'animal life,' need food in the state of innocence, unlike the future resurrected life?
options: Because food was needed only for pleasure, with no bodily necessity behind it

Because the rational soul, called 'soul' insofar as it gives life to the body (as with other living things) and 'spirit' insofar as it possesses intellectual power, in the state of innocence still lived an animal bodily life requiring nourishment, whereas after the resurrection life will be wholly spiritual, needing no food
Because Adam was punished with hunger immediately upon creation, before any sin
Because food in paradise served no biological function and was purely symbolic of moral virtue
P1Q97.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the soul's role as 'soul' (giving bodily life, requiring nourishment as in other living things) from its role as 'spirit' (its properly intellectual power); in the state of innocence man still had this animal, food-dependent life, unlike the wholly spiritual life to come after the resurrection.

P1Q97.q: How did the tree of life function as a 'cause of immortality,' according to Aquinas?
options: It granted immortality automatically and absolutely to anyone who ate from it even once, regardless of ongoing need

It served as a remedy against the natural decline whereby the active power of the human species is gradually weakened by the admixture of extraneous nutriment (as water dilutes wine), strengthening the specific active force against this decline so as to ward off old age's corruption—not as an absolute, but a real contributing cause
It caused immortality by magically transforming the body into an immaterial substance
It had no real effect on the body and was purely a symbol with no causal role, per Aquinas's clear denial
P1Q97.explanation: Aquinas explains, citing Augustine, that the tree of life countered the gradual weakening of the body's active generative/nutritive force caused by the accumulation of assimilated extraneous matter (like water diluting wine)—strengthening the species' vital force against the decline leading to old age and death, functioning as a real but not absolute cause of immortality.

P1Q98.q: Why does Aquinas insist that generation of offspring would have occurred in the state of innocence, even without sin?
options: Because without sin there would have been no purpose for humans to multiply at all

Because otherwise the multiplication of the human race—a great blessing—would have required sin as its necessary condition, which is absurd; man's body, naturally corruptible though his soul is naturally incorruptible, requires generation for the perpetuation of the species, which is nature's chief purpose for corruptible things
Because Aquinas holds that Adam and Eve were never actually intended to have children at all
Because Scripture states generation began only after the expulsion from Eden, which Aquinas simply repeats without comment
P1Q98.explanation: Aquinas argues it would be absurd for so great a blessing as the multiplication of the human race to depend on sin as a necessary condition; since man's body is naturally corruptible, generation—nature's chief purpose for corruptible things—would still have been needed to preserve the human species even without sin.

P1Q98.q: How does Aquinas respond to the view (attributed to Gregory of Nyssa) that generation in paradise would have occurred without coition, as with the angels?
options: He fully agrees, holding that coition is entirely a result of sin, not integral to human animal nature

He rejects it as unreasonable, since what is natural to man was neither acquired nor forfeited by sin, and generation by coition is natural to man by reason of his animal life, which he possessed even before sin, as shown by the natural fittedness of the corporeal members involved
He is uncertain and refuses to take any position on this question
He agrees only regarding Adam, but not regarding Eve
P1Q98.explanation: Aquinas rejects Gregory of Nyssa's view as unreasonable, arguing that what belongs naturally to man's animal life (which predates sin) cannot have been acquired or lost through sin; since coition is natural to man's animal life and the bodily members are naturally fitted for it, it would have occurred even without sin.

P1Q99.q: Would children born in the state of innocence have had full use of their limbs immediately after birth, according to Aquinas's natural reasoning?
options: Yes, absolutely and necessarily so, since this belongs to nature apart from any special divine gift

By nature, no—it is natural and fitting to human nature that children lack full use of their limbs at birth (given the brain's greater relative size and moisture in humans, affecting the nerves), though Aquinas notes that no Catholic doubts God could grant a child use of its limbs immediately by His power
No, children in paradise would have been permanently unable to move their limbs their whole lives
The question is entirely inapplicable since no children would have existed in paradise
P1Q99.explanation: Aquinas argues from natural principles that human children naturally lack full use of their limbs at birth due to the brain's relative size and moisture affecting nerve function, while acknowledging this could have been supernaturally altered by divine power, though nature's ordinary course is his guide absent special revelation.

P1Q99.q: Would both sexes have been born in the state of innocence, according to Aquinas?
options: No, only males would have been born, since femininity was considered by Aquinas a post-Fall defect

Yes, since nothing belonging to the completeness of human nature would have been lacking in paradise, and just as diverse grades belong to the perfection of the universe, diversity of sex belongs to the perfection of human nature itself
No, humans in paradise would have reproduced asexually with no distinction of sex at birth
The question is left completely undecided by Aquinas, with no argument given either way
P1Q99.explanation: Aquinas argues that the completeness of human nature would not have been lacking in the sinless state, and since diversity of sex belongs to the perfection of human nature (paralleling how diverse grades belong to the perfection of the universe), both sexes would have been born in paradise.

P1Q100.q: Would children in the state of innocence have been born possessing original righteousness, according to Aquinas?
options: No, original righteousness was a purely personal, non-transmissible gift to Adam alone with no bearing on offspring

Yes; since man naturally begets a likeness of himself, and original righteousness was a gift conferred not merely on Adam personally but on the whole human nature (as shown by original sin, its opposite, being transmitted as 'the sin of nature'), children would have been assimilated to their parents in original righteousness as well
Children's righteousness would have been entirely random and unrelated to their parents' state
Original righteousness applies only to angels, not to human offspring at all
P1Q100.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since original righteousness was a gift given to the whole of human nature (not merely as an individual accident), and since its opposite, original sin, is transmitted to offspring precisely because it is 'the sin of nature,' children in the state of innocence would likewise have been born possessing original righteousness like their parents.

P1Q100.q: Would children have been born already confirmed in righteousness (unable to sin), according to Aquinas?
options: Yes, since original righteousness is itself equivalent to confirmation in grace

No; since children at birth would not have had greater perfection than their parents possessed while begetting them, and the parents themselves, so long as they were still generating children (an act of animal life), had not yet attained the beatific vision that alone confirms a rational creature unshakably in righteousness
Yes, because Aquinas holds that confirmation in righteousness happens automatically at conception
The question does not arise because Aquinas denies there would have been any children at all
P1Q100.explanation: Aquinas argues that children could not have greater perfection at birth than their parents had while begetting them, and since the parents (while still engaged in the animal-life act of generation) had not yet received the beatific vision that alone confirms a creature unshakably in righteousness, their children would not have been born already confirmed.
